name: Matcha Latte
instructions: Sift matcha powder into a bowl to remove clumps.
Add hot water and whisk vigorously in a W-motion until frothy.
Heat and froth the milk.
Pour milk over the matcha.
Sweeten to taste and serve immediately.
tips: Water should be around 80°C — boiling water makes matcha bitter.

name: Yuzu Honey Drink
instructions: Mix yuzu juice and honey until the honey dissolves.
Add hot water for a warm drink, or sparkling water + ice for a cold version.
Stir well and serve.
tips: Fresh yuzu is ideal, but good bottled pure yuzu juice works year-round.

name: Hojicha Latte
instructions: Steep or whisk hojicha with hot water.
Heat and froth the milk.
Pour milk over the hojicha.
Sweeten if desired and serve.
tips: Hojicha has a roasted, nutty flavor and is naturally lower in caffeine than matcha.

name: Genmaicha Tea

ingredients.name: Genmaicha (green tea with roasted brown rice)

instructions: Place genmaicha in a teapot or infuser.
Pour hot (not boiling) water over the leaves.
Steep 1–2 minutes.
Serve hot, or cool and pour over ice for a cold version.
tips: The roasted rice gives a nutty, comforting aroma. Very easy everyday Japanese tea.

name: Amazake (Sweet Fermented Rice Drink)

ingredients.name: Store-bought amazake or homemade rice koji amazake

instructions: Gently warm the amazake with water or milk (do not boil).
Add a little grated ginger if desired.
Serve warm in small cups.
tips: A traditional sweet, non-alcoholic fermented rice drink — naturally creamy and comforting.

name: Sakura Latte (Cherry Blossom Latte)

ingredients.name: Sakura (cherry blossom) syrup or salted sakura
Optional: a little matcha or just plain

instructions: Warm the milk and froth it.
Add sakura syrup to a cup.
Pour the frothed milk over the syrup.
Stir gently and serve. Can be served hot or iced.
tips: A seasonal Japanese café favorite. Salted pickled sakura gives a unique floral-salty note.

name: Bubble Tea (Boba)
instructions: Cook tapioca pearls according to package, then soak in syrup.
Brew strong black tea and let it cool.
Add pearls to the bottom of a glass, add ice.
Pour tea and milk over the ice.
Serve with a wide straw.
tips: Use brown sugar syrup for the classic caramel flavor that coats the pearls.

name: Chrysanthemum Tea
instructions: Place chrysanthemum flowers (and goji berries if using) in a teapot or glass.
Pour hot water over them and steep 3–5 minutes.
Add rock sugar or honey to taste.
Serve hot or chilled over ice.
tips: Traditionally believed to help cool the body and clear the eyes.

name: Eight Treasure Tea (Ba Bao Cha)
instructions: Place all dried ingredients in a teapot or heatproof glass.
Pour boiling water over them.
Steep 5–10 minutes until the water turns golden and fragrant.
Add rock sugar to taste.
Refill with hot water several times — the flavor develops with each steep.
tips: A traditional Chinese herbal tea believed to nourish the body.

name: Homemade Soy Milk

ingredients.name: Sugar or a pinch of salt

instructions: Soak soybeans overnight, then blend with water until smooth.
Strain through a cheesecloth or nut milk bag.
Cook the milk over medium heat, stirring constantly, until it boils.
Simmer a few more minutes, then sweeten or salt to taste.
Serve hot in winter or chilled in summer.
tips: Fresh homemade soy milk tastes much better than boxed versions.

name: Osmanthus Tea
instructions: Place osmanthus flowers in a glass or teapot.
Pour hot water over and steep 3–5 minutes.
Add rock sugar or honey to taste.
Serve hot or lightly chilled.
tips: Osmanthus has a delicate floral, apricot-like aroma — very fragrant and refined.

name: Winter Melon Tea

ingredients.name: Optional: a few dried longan or goji

instructions: Boil winter melon cubes with water until soft and the liquid turns slightly cloudy.
Add rock sugar and optional dried fruits.
Simmer a few more minutes, then strain or serve with the soft melon.
Serve hot or chilled.
tips: A classic Chinese cooling drink, especially popular in summer.

name: Sikhye (Sweet Rice Punch)
instructions: Mix cooked rice with malt powder and warm water.
Let sit at warm room temperature for several hours until a few grains float.
Strain the liquid, add sugar, and heat gently.
Cool completely and refrigerate.
Serve cold with a few rice grains and pine nuts.
tips: Traditionally served after meals to aid digestion. Store-bought sikhye is also widely available.

name: Misugaru (Roasted Grain Shake)
instructions: Add misugaru powder to a shaker or blender.
Pour in milk or water and sweetener.
Shake or blend until smooth and frothy.
Add ice if you want it cold.
Serve immediately.
tips: A popular healthy Korean breakfast or snack drink made from roasted grains and beans.

name: Omija Tea (Five-Flavor Berry Tea)
instructions: Simmer dried omija berries in water for 10–15 minutes.
Strain the bright red liquid.
Sweeten with honey while still warm.
Serve hot or chilled over ice.
Garnish with a few pine nuts if desired.
tips: Omija means ‘five flavors’ — sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and pungent.

name: Barley Tea (Bori-cha)
instructions: Toast the barley lightly in a dry pan if not pre-roasted.
Add to a pot of water and bring to a boil.
Simmer 10–15 minutes until the water turns light brown and fragrant.
Strain and serve hot or chilled.
tips: A classic everyday Korean table drink — caffeine-free, nutty, and very refreshing when cold.

name: Banana Milk (Korean-style)
instructions: Blend bananas with milk, sweetener, and vanilla until smooth.
Add ice and blend again if you want it colder.
Pour into glasses and serve immediately.
tips: Inspired by the popular Korean banana milk drinks — simple, creamy, and kid-friendly.

name: Corn Silk Tea (Oksusu Suyeomcha)
instructions: Rinse the corn silk and place in a pot with water.
Bring to a boil, then simmer 15–20 minutes until the water turns light golden.
Strain and sweeten lightly if desired.
Serve hot or cold.
tips: A traditional Korean herbal tea often drunk for its mild, sweet, and cleansing qualities.

name: Calamansi Juice
instructions: Juice the calamansi and strain out the seeds.
Mix juice with water and sugar until dissolved.
Pour over ice.
Serve immediately. Adjust sweetness to taste.
tips: Calamansi is smaller and more aromatic than regular limes — the classic Filipino citrus drink.

name: Sago Gulaman
instructions: Cook sago until translucent, rinse and set aside.
Prepare gulaman according to package, cool, and cube.
Make syrup by boiling brown sugar with water until slightly thickened.
In a glass: add sago, gulaman cubes, ice, then pour syrup and cold water.
Mix and serve cold.
tips: You can add coconut water or pineapple juice for extra tropical flavor.

name: Buko Juice (Young Coconut Juice)

ingredients.name: Optional: buko strips from the same coconut

instructions: Open the young coconuts and pour the water into a pitcher.
Scrape out the soft coconut meat.
Add ice and sweetener if desired.
Add the coconut strips back into the juice.
Serve immediately with a straw and spoon.
tips: Best when the coconut is very young and the meat is soft and jelly-like.

name: Ginger Tea (Salabat)
instructions: Boil ginger in water for 10–15 minutes until fragrant and strong.
Strain into cups.
Sweeten with brown sugar or honey.
Add a squeeze of calamansi if desired.
Serve hot.
tips: A classic Filipino remedy and everyday comfort drink, especially during rainy or cold weather.

name: Melon Juice
instructions: Scoop out the melon flesh and blend until smooth.
Add water or milk and sweetener, blend again.
Strain if you prefer a smoother texture.
Pour over ice and serve cold.
tips: A very common Filipino merienda drink — sweet, cold, and hydrating.

name: Tsokolate (Tablea Hot Chocolate)
instructions: Dissolve tablea in hot water or milk over low heat, whisking constantly.
Use a molinillo or whisk to make it frothy.
Sweeten with sugar or condensed milk.
Serve hot and thick.
tips: Traditional Filipino hot chocolate made from pure tablea — rich, slightly bitter, and deeply comforting.

name: Thai Iced Tea (Cha Yen)
instructions: Steep Thai tea mix in hot water for 5 minutes.
Strain, add sugar while hot, and stir until dissolved.
Let cool, then pour over a glass full of ice.
Top with evaporated milk.
Serve with a straw.
tips: The iconic orange color comes from the food coloring in authentic Thai tea mix.

name: Thai Coconut Water with Jelly

ingredients.name: Nata de coco or grass jelly

instructions: Open young coconut and pour the water into a pitcher.
Scoop out the soft coconut meat.
Add coconut meat, jelly, and ice to glasses.
Pour coconut water over and sweeten lightly if desired.
Serve immediately with a spoon and straw.
tips: Fresh young coconut water is best, but good-quality bottled versions work in a pinch.

name: Thai Iced Coffee (Oliang)

ingredients.name: Thai coffee mix or strong dark coffee

instructions: Brew strong Thai coffee or dark roast coffee.
Stir in condensed milk while hot.
Fill a glass with ice.
Pour the coffee over ice and top with evaporated milk.
Stir and enjoy.
tips: Authentic Thai coffee often uses a cloth bag filter for a smoother brew.

name: Nam Dok Anchan (Butterfly Pea Lemonade)
instructions: Steep butterfly pea flowers in hot water until the liquid turns deep blue.
Strain and cool.
Add sweetener and pour over ice.
Add lime juice — the color will change to purple/pink.
Serve and watch the color magic.
tips: A beautiful Thai herbal drink. The color change when acid is added is always a crowd-pleaser.

name: Thai Lemongrass Drink

ingredients.name: Optional: a few slices of ginger or pandan

instructions: Smash the lemongrass and simmer in water for 10–15 minutes.
Strain, sweeten while still warm.
Cool and serve over ice.
Can also be served hot.
tips: Light, citrusy, and naturally caffeine-free — a very common Thai homemade drink.

name: Roselle Juice (Nam Krajeab)

ingredients.name: Optional: a few slices of ginger

instructions: Boil roselle flowers with water (and optional ginger) for 10–15 minutes.
Strain the deep red liquid.
Sweeten while still warm.
Cool and serve over ice.
tips: A popular Thai herbal drink with a tart, cranberry-like flavor and beautiful red color.
